title: US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
content:
US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
Former White House staffer calls for espionage and cyber options as Washington prepares for a potential Chinese breakthrough
Jacob Stokes, deputy director of the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said at an online event on Thursday that various US agencies, including the Department of Defense and the National Security Agency, should begin assessing what intelligence they need to justify taking such actions.
“Trying to think through the particulars of that will be especially important, in part because it will help policymakers … start to work backwards based on the unique nature of the technology, in the same way that in a past era, policymakers would learn about nuclear weapons and … work backwards from the science to the policy implications,” he said.
In a new CNAS report published last week, the former Obama administration national security staffer called for the US government to consider the feasibility of diplomatic, espionage, cyber and kinetic measures to prevent China from achieving AGI first.

report.summary: Former US official urges planning for espionage, cyber, and military options to prevent China from achieving AGI first.
report.background: The report stems from growing US-China competition over artificial intelligence, particularly the race toward artificial general intelligence (AGI), which many experts believe could fundamentally shift global power. Jacob Stokes, a former Obama administration national security staffer and now deputy director at CNAS, argues that the United States must proactively assess intelligence requirements and policy options in case China appears close to an AGI breakthrough. His comments echo historical frameworks used during the nuclear era, when policymakers worked backward from scientific possibilities to design containment strategies. The proposal reflects a broader debate in Washington about whether AGI is a national security asset so critical that preemptive measures—including kinetic action—should be considered, despite severe risks and ethical concerns.
key_points: A CNAS report urges US agencies like the Pentagon and NSA to identify what intelligence would be needed to justify actions—ranging from diplomacy to military strikes—if China appears poised to achieve AGI first.
Stokes compares AGI to nuclear weapons, saying policymakers should study the technology's unique characteristics now to prepare responses, rather than reacting after a breakthrough occurs.
The proposal explicitly includes espionage, cyber operations, and kinetic measures, sparking debate over whether such extreme steps are realistic, proportionate, or dangerously escalatory.
The report signals that AGI is being treated not just as an economic or technological issue but as a top-tier national security priority in an era of intense US-China strategic rivalry.
Skeptics note that AGI is hypothetical and difficult to define, making preemptive military planning both speculative and risky, especially given the global interdependence of AI research.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this rhetoric could accelerate government scrutiny of research collaborations, export controls, and talent flows between countries. Developers may face tighter restrictions on sharing models, datasets, or computing resources internationally. For regular users, public discourse might shift from AGI’s societal benefits to fears of a zero-sum race, potentially justifying greater state surveillance or limiting open access. If governments seriously pursue preemptive measures, the AI field could become militarized, fragmenting global research and slowing progress. However, most analysts view actual military strikes as extreme and unlikely; the report more likely aims to pressure policymakers into strategic planning and intelligence prioritization.
report.tools: Observers should monitor Center for a New American Security (CNAS) reports on AI and Indo-Pacific security, and policy trackers from the US Department of Defense and National Security Agency on AI. For technical context, follow open-source AI efforts like EleutherAI’s GPT-NeoX or Hugging Face’s model registries, as they illustrate global AI diffusion that complicates any attempt to control breakthroughs.
